## Background: The Miracle of Liver Regeneration

- The liver's capacity to regenerate is unique in the human body
- Captivated mankind since ancient civilizations (e.g., Greek myths of Tityus and Prometheus)
- Twenty-seven centuries later, physicians manipulate this regenerative capacity to treat oncologic liver diseases
- Goal: To cure, not to torture as in ancient myths

## What is ALPPS?

- **ALPPS** stands for:
  - **A**ssociating
  - **L**iver
  - **P**artition and
  - **P**ortal vein ligation for
  - **S**taged hepatectomy

- A two-stage strategy to induce rapid and massive future liver remnant (FLR) hypertrophy
- Reduces the usual time interval between stages to **1 or 2 weeks**
- Allows resection of liver tumors otherwise functionally irresectable

## Figure 123.2: Diagram of ALPPS Stages

::: {.callout-note}
## The Two-Stage Concept
**Stage 1:**
- Division of the right portal vein
- Resection/ablation of tumors in the FLR (if present)
- Splitting of the parenchyma according to the future resection type

**Stage 2:**
- Division of the right hepatic artery, right bile duct, and right venous drainage
- Allows resection of the tumor-bearing liver
:::

## History: The First ALPPS (2007)

- Performed somewhat incidentally by **Prof. Hans J. Schlitt** (Regensburg, Germany) in September 2007
- **Patient:** 49-year-old female with hilar cholangiocarcinoma
- **Scheduled procedure:** Right trisectionectomy
- **Original plan:** Right portal vein transection + complete in situ splitting along the falciform ligament

## The First Case: Intraoperative Pivot

- The middle hepatic vein (MHV) was taken down, but hepatic arteries were untouched
- After complete transection, the FLR seemed critical and insufficient
- **Plan canceled:** Resection was stopped without removing the tumor
- A Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy to the left lateral lobe was performed to decompress segments II and III

## The First Case: The Result

- **1 week later:** CT scan showed an almost **doubling in volume** of segments II and III (the FLR)
- **Day 9:** Returned to the OR; trisectionectomy plus resection of the hilar bifurcation was completed
- **Outcome:** Uneventful postoperative course without liver insufficiency (though early tumor relapse occurred)

## Evolution of the Name

- The technique was initially termed **"in situ-split liver resection"**
- Soon adopted by other HPB centers in Germany
- **2011:** First report of 5 cases presented at the E-AHPBA congress in Capetown
- **2012:** Multicenter inaugural report of 25 cases published in *Annals of Surgery*
- **Naming:** Eduardo de Santibañes and Pierre Clavien suggested the acronym **ALPPS** to avoid confusion with segmental liver transplantation partition

## The International ALPPS Registry

- Created in **2012** due to increasing interest and passion for the concept
- **Founding members:** P. A. Clavien, H. Lang, and E. de Santibañes
- Goal: Collect data on this new procedure from centers worldwide
- Currently comprises over **1250 patients**

## Initial Hype vs. Reality

- ALPPS pushed the limits of resection into a new dimension
- Seemed to offer an almost **100% resection rate** for tumors considered irresectable due to insufficient FLR
- **Median hypertrophy rates:** 160% and up to 250%
- Even allowed resection of all but one segment (**monosegment ALPPS**)

## The Slowdown: Facing the Risks

- Initial hype slowed down due to **very high initial perioperative surgical risk**
- Inaugural multicenter German experience showed **12% mortality**
- Concerns raised: Was the increase in resectability bought at the expense of safety?
- Most deaths occurred after **Stage 2**
- Main cause of poor outcomes: **Posthepatectomy liver failure (PHLF)**, paradoxically even when sufficient FLR volumes were achieved

## Risk Factors for Poor Outcomes

- Post-Stage 1 complications (Grade $\ge$ 3b) are significant predictors of Stage 2 mortality
- Specific risk factors:
  - Post-Stage 1 biliary fistula
  - Infected and/or bilious peritoneal fluid at Stage 2
  - Pre-Stage 2 **bilirubin** and **creatinine** levels

## Figure 123.3: Timeline of ALPPS Development

::: {.callout-note}
## Evolution of Techniques (2007 to 2020+)
**More aggressive Stage 1:**
- Classic ALPPS (2007)

**Less aggressive Stage 1 (Technical Refinements):**
- Tourniquet ALPPS (2012)
- Partial ALPPS (2014)
- RFA / Microwave ALPPS (2015)
- Mini ALPPS (2016)
:::

## Anatomic Considerations: Overview

The main components of ALPPS (regardless of modification) are:
1. Interruption of Portal Vein (PV) circulation
2. Manipulation of liver parenchyma along the transection line
3. The two stages of the operation

**Core Concept:** Complete portal devascularization of the tumor-carrying liver, while preserving arterial flow and intact vascularization/biliary drainage of the FLR.

## Preoperative Imaging is Mandatory

- High proportion of vasculobiliary variants requires precise anatomic knowledge
- Imaging must assess the FLR and all individual anatomic details
- Tumors frequently alter normal anatomy in advanced liver diseases

## Hepatic Artery: Crucial Preservation

- At Stage 1, preservation of arterial inflow to **both sides** (remnant and specimen) is crucial
- Lesions or occlusion of the HA can cause necrosis and failure of the procedure
- Special attention in right trisectionectomy to the **"middle HA"** and branches supplying **Segment IV**

## Figure 123.4: Arterial Variants of Segment IV

::: {.callout-note}
## Vascularization of Segment IV
**(A)** Segment IV artery originating early from the left hepatic artery (**40%**)
**(B)** Segment IV artery originating from the left hepatic artery in the umbilical fissure (**35%**)
**(C)** Segment IV artery originating from the right hepatic artery (**25%**)

*Preservation of perfusion to Segment IV is imperative to avoid ischemic complications.*
:::

## Portal Vein: The Key Interruption

- Interruption of specimen-side portal inflow is the key to ALPPS
- Variants mainly refer to the right side
- Must distinguish single PV branching/trifurcation from truly abnormal configurations
- Missing a portal branch during Stage 1 can occur in true aberrant branches (e.g., right anterior sectorial branch from the left branch)

## Figure 123.5: Portal Vein Trunk Variants

::: {.callout-note}
## PV Anatomy Variations
**(A)** Trifurcation (8%)
**(B)** Early origin of the right-posterior (RP) branch (10%)
**(C)** Right-anterior (RA) branch from the left (L) branch (2.7%)
**(D)** Separate segmental branches of RA and RP (1%)
**(E)** Complex anatomy with a single nonbifurcating PV (1%)
:::

## Hepatic Vein: Venous Drainage

- Runs via right, middle, and left hepatic veins (HVs)
- Middle and left form a common trunk in ~90% of cases
- **Inferior Right Hepatic Vein (IRHV):** Drains segment VI; usually smaller than RHV but occasionally larger
- **Middle Hepatic Vein (MHV):** Drains 20-30% of total liver volume (segments IVa/b, V, VIII). A dominant MHV may drain up to 50%.

## Bile Duct: A Major Source of Morbidity

- Biliary tree shows multiple variations in division and course
- Precise knowledge is of **utmost importance** as biliary complications are a major source of postoperative morbidity and mortality in ALPPS
- A single left hepatic duct is present in 98% of cases
- Crossing right bile ducts (e.g., right-posterior entering left hepatic duct) occur in ~5% of cases

## Figure 123.6 & 123.7: Biliary Variations

::: {.callout-note}
## Segment IV and Hepatic Duct Confluence
- **Segment IV Biliary Drainage:** Highly variable. A separate Segment IV duct is present in ~57% of cases, but common trunks with Seg II or III occur frequently.
- **Hepatic Duct Confluence:** Typical anatomy is common, but variations like a right posterior duct crossing to the left system require careful mapping to prevent catastrophic leaks or strictures.
:::

## Patient Selection: General Principles

- Eligible for ALPPS on a case-by-case basis within a multidisciplinary tumor board
- Indicated when an **insufficient FLR** (considering volume and function) is present
- Despite being applied for any liver tumor initially, **Colorectal Liver Metastases (CRLM)** remains the indication of choice

## Preoperative Workup and Volumetry

- State-of-the-art imaging (multislice CT / MRI) with 3D reconstruction
- **Total Liver Volume (TLV)** and **FLR volume** are mandatory
- **FLR Inadequacy Cutoffs:**
  - < 30% of TLV in healthy livers
  - < 40% in patients with cholestasis, macrosteatosis, fibrosis, or long-course chemotherapy
- **FLR-to-Body Weight Ratio:** < 0.5% (normal), < 0.8% (abnormal), < 1.4% (cirrhotic)

## Functional Assessment: Beyond Volume

- FLR volume does not necessarily reflect function (hepatocyte function might be impaired)
- **Nuclear imaging techniques** (e.g., 99mTc-mebrofenin hepatobiliary scintigraphy - HBS) measure both volume and sectorial FLR function
- **AMC Cutoff:** FLR function corrected for body surface area of **2.7%/min/m2** predicts PHLF

## Specific Indications for ALPPS over PVE

To get the best from ALPPS, restrict to patients with insufficient FLR AND at least one of:
1. Tumor margin close to the FLR or its vascular pedicles
2. Bilobar disease with contraindication for PVE as a single-stage strategy
3. Need for large hypertrophy (> 65%) in an extremely small FLR
4. HBS FLR uptake rate < 1.7/min/m2 (unlikely to reach sufficient function after PVE)
5. **Failure of PVE/PVL** ("Rescue ALPPS")

## Surgical Technique: Classic ALPPS Stage 1

- **Exploration & Ultrasound:** Careful palpation and IOUS of the FLR; resect any tumors in the FLR
- **Mobilization:** Complete mobilization; caudate lobe freed from IVC; cholecystectomy performed
- **Portal Vein:** PV of the diseased hemiliver is divided
- **Transection:** Total parenchymal transection up to the IVC

## The Challenge of Segment IV

- In right trisectionectomy, Segment IV vascularization is crucial
- Small portal branches to Seg IVa/b must be taken down
- **Arterial supply to Seg IV MUST be preserved** to avoid ischemia, necrosis, and infection
- Anatomic intraglissonian dissection at the umbilical groove is recommended

## Figure 123.10: Glissonian Segment IV Pedicle

::: {.callout-note}
## A Risky Maneuver
- Ligation of a glissonian Segment IV pedicle emerging from the right side of the umbilical fissure using the hanging maneuver.
- *Current consensus:* Ligation of these specific pedicles is considered **risky and unnecessary** in right trisectionectomy ALPPS, as it threatens Segment IV viability.
:::

## Partial ALPPS: A Safer Alternative

- Original ALPPS included taking down the MHV and complete transection
- **Partial ALPPS:** Preserves the MHV and parts of surrounding tissue; incomplete parenchymal transection (~50% depth)
- **Benefits:**
  - Reduces risk of involuntary section of Seg IV bile ducts
  - Reduces biliary leaks
  - Results in similar velocity/extent of hypertrophy
  - **Significant reduction in perioperative morbidity**

## Figure 123.11: Partial ALPPS Stage 1

::: {.callout-note}
## Visualizing Partial Transection
- About 50% splitting of liver parenchyma along the right side of the falciform ligament.
- Light blue vascular tags mark the right main glissonian pedicle and right hepatic vein.
- Cystic duct cannulated for transcystic hydraulic test and cholangiography.
:::

## Biliary Management in Stage 1

- Perform transcystic hydraulic test, air-bubble test, or cholangiography to prevent leaks
- **Bile duct ligation to the future specimen should NOT be performed** (leads to cholestasis, infection, leaks)
- Manipulate the biliary tree as little as possible
- Necessary reconstructions (e.g., hepaticojejunostomy) should be deferred to Stage 2 if possible

## Ending Stage 1

- Mark tumor-carrying liver vasculobiliary structures with silk ties or vessel loops (anatomy changes due to atrophy/hypertrophy)
- Cover cut surfaces with hemostatic sheets to prevent adhesions (plastic bags are now abandoned)
- Place two drains: one between transection lines, one in the right subphrenic space

## Classic ALPPS Stage 2

- Careful exploration, release adhesions, extensive washout
- Intraabdominal swab for microbiologic analysis
- Identify hilar structures using vascular tags
- Resect tumor-bearing lobe (staplers for vascular/glissonian structures)
- IOUS to check perfusion; refixation of falciform ligament
- **Intraoperative test for bile leaks is strongly recommended**

## Figure 123.14: Beginning of Stage 2

::: {.callout-note}
## Stage 2 Execution
**(A)** Adhesions broken up; light blue tags easily recognized (RHV, glissonian pedicle, HA, cystic duct).
**(B)** Intraparenchymal glissonian division using a vascular stapler.
**(C)** Hypertrophied FLR seen after resection.
**(D)** Final cholangiogram to rule out leaks.
:::

## Monosegment ALPPS: Pushing the Limits

- **Definition:** Liver resection leaving a remnant of **1 single segment** (plus/minus Segment I)
- Overcomes left and right trisectionectomy limits
- First introduced in 2015 (Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires) leaving only Segments I and IV
- Challenges the basic rule requiring preservation of at least two contiguous Couinaud segments

## Types of Monosegment ALPPS

1. **S2 ALPPS:** Seg III resected in Stage 1 $\rightarrow$ Right trisectionectomy in Stage 2
2. **S3 ALPPS:** Seg II resected in Stage 1 $\rightarrow$ Right trisectionectomy in Stage 2
3. **S4 ALPPS:** Left lateral segment removed in Stage 1 $\rightarrow$ Right hepatectomy in Stage 2
4. **S6 ALPPS:** Requires anatomic variant (IRHV draining Seg VI) $\rightarrow$ Most challenging

## Figure 123.15 & 123.16: Monosegment ALPPS

::: {.callout-note}
## Extreme Hypertrophy
**Figure 123.15 (Seg IV):** Liver partition at Cantlie's line, left lateral sectionectomy performed. FLR comprises only Seg IV and I.
**Figure 123.16 (Seg II):** End of Stage 1 after Seg III resection. Stage 2 shows a massively hypertrophied Segment II FLR after extended right trisectionectomy.
:::

## Technical Variations: Overview

To improve outcomes and reduce Stage 1 trauma, several variations have been introduced:
- Tourniquet ALPPS
- Microwave / Radiofrequency ALPPS
- Hybrid ALPPS
- Mini ALPPS
- Laparoscopic ALPPS

*Less invasive Stage 1 techniques are confirmed as an independent factor related to decreased mortality.*

## Tourniquet ALPPS

- Introduced by Robles et al. (Murcia, Spain)
- Replaces transection with a **tourniquet** applied around the liver in a 1 cm parenchymal groove
- Tourniquet passed via the hanging maneuver (in front of IVC)
- Must be knotted tightly enough to completely occlude interlobar circulation (verified by IOUS)

## Microwave and Radiofrequency ALPPS

- Replaces parenchymal transection with thermal ablation
- Creates a liver partition through a **"necrotic groove"**
- Performed under IOUS guidance above major intrahepatic glissonian pedicles (40-60 mm depth)
- Can be performed minimally invasively (laparoscopic or percutaneous)
- **REBIRTH trial:** RFA-ALPPS produced significantly greater volume increase in shorter time than PVE, without increased morbidity

## Hybrid ALPPS

- Replaces surgical Portal Vein Ligation (PVL) with **Portal Vein Embolization (PVE)** during the interval period
- Avoids portal pedicle dissection during Stage 1 ("no-touch" oncologic principle)
- Facilitates Stage 2 (fewer adhesions, easier hilar identification)
- Useful in PV variants where surgical occlusion is technically demanding

## Mini ALPPS: A Paradigm Shift

- Combines three concepts:
  1. Partial parenchymal transection
  2. Intraoperative transmesenteric PVE
  3. "No-touch" oncologic rules (avoiding portal pedicle dissection and liver mobilization)
- **Result:** Dramatically reduces surgical impact of Stage 1; main surgical steps shifted to Stage 2

## Figure 123.17: Mini ALPPS Technique

::: {.callout-note}
## The Mini ALPPS Steps
**(A)** Partial transection in the dome (depth 3-5 cm) to avoid MHV and Seg IV branches.
**(B)** Intraoperative transmesenteric PVE via the inferior mesenteric vein (IMV).
**(C)** Untouched hepatoduodenal ligament and gallbladder found at Stage 2.
**(D)** Schematic of the technique.
:::

## Laparoscopic Mini ALPPS

- Intraoperative transmesenteric PVE adapted for laparoscopy
- Innovative technique: Laparoscopic-assisted percutaneous cannulation of the IMV using a 5-Fr introducer (Seldinger technique)
- Adds benefits of minimally invasive surgery to the reduced trauma of Mini ALPPS

## Figure 123.18: Laparoscopic Mini ALPPS

::: {.callout-note}
## Minimally Invasive Execution
**(A)** Partial transection without right liver mobilization.
**(B)** IMV individualized near the ligament of Treitz.
**(C)** Laparoscopic-assisted percutaneous cannulation of IMV.
**(D)** Trocar disposition and percutaneous sheath insertion.
**(E)** Interval CT showing FLR hypertrophy and embolization material.
:::

## Table 123.1: Main Surgical Characteristics of Stage 1

| Technique | PV Occlusion | Parenchymal Interruption | Liver Mobilization |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Classic** | Ligation/division | Complete transection | Full |
| **Tourniquet** | Ligation/division | Tourniquet | Anterior approach |
| **Hybrid** | Interval PVE | Partial transection | Anterior approach |
| **Partial** | Ligation/division | Partial transection | Anterior approach |
| **MWA/RFA** | Ligation/division | Thermal ablation | Anterior approach |
| **Mini** | IO transmesenteric PVE | Partial transection | Anterior approach |

## Interval Management: Volume vs. Function

- Patient management between stages is key
- Remnant volume is a predictor of PHLF, but **volume may increase rapidly and precede functional recovery**
- Initial edema and hepatocyte immaturity occur in the first 2 weeks
- **Discrepancy:** Rapid volume increase does not equal immediate functional sufficiency
- **Conclusion:** Must assess liver *function* in addition to volume

## Assessing FLR Function

- **Hepatobiliary Scintigraphy (HBS)** combined with SPECT-CT offers quantitative segmental liver function
- **AMC Cutoff:** Wait until FLR uptake rate reaches **2.7%/min/m2**
- **HIBA Index:** Modern HBS assessment cutoff of **> 15%**
- **Kinetic Growth Rate (KGR):** A KGR < 4.1% per day predicts PHLF after Stage 2

## Figure 123.19: Perioperative FLR Assessment

::: {.callout-note}
## Merging Volume and Function
**(A)** Baseline CT volumetry of Seg II FLR.
**(B)** Interval CT showing 170% hypertrophy at Day 6.
**(C)** Merging CT with 99mTc-mebrofenin HBS using SPECT.
**(D)** Provides accurate 3D regional distribution of liver function, preventing futile Stage 2 operations.
:::

## Timing of Stage 2

- The initial "1-week interval dogma" has been penalized with high complication rates
- **Delay or abandon Stage 2 if:**
  - Compromised clinical status
  - Active complications
  - Abnormal liver function tests
  - MELD score > 10
- Patients can be discharged home and readmitted once FLR sufficiency and low risk score are achieved

## The ALPPS Risk Score

- Created in 2016 from the ALPPS Registry to predict 90-day/in-hospital mortality
- **Pre-Stage 2 Model Variables:**
  - Pre-Stage 1 score
  - Interstage complications $\ge$ 3b
  - Serum bilirubin pre-Stage 2
  - Serum creatinine pre-Stage 2
- Predicts futility risk (5% to 50% based on scores 3.9 to 6.9)

## Figure 123.20: Selection and Management Flowchart

::: {.callout-note}
## Algorithm for ALPPS
1. **Indication:** Insufficient FLR + specific criteria (close margin, bilobar, PVE failure).
2. **Stage 1:** Perform ALPPS.
3. **Day 6 Assessment:** CT/MRI Volumetry + HBS.
4. **Decision:**
   - If HIBA-i $\ge$ 15% / AMC-i $\ge$ 2.7 $\rightarrow$ Proceed to Stage 2 (if clinical condition is good, MELD < 10).
   - If functional criteria not met $\rightarrow$ Delay surgery and reassess weekly.
:::

## ALPPS for Colorectal Liver Metastases (CRLM)

- **Best-established indication** (almost two-thirds of registry cases)
- Morbidity/mortality comparable to conventional major hepatectomies
- 3-year OS and DFS: 50% and 13% respectively
- **LIGRO Trial:** Randomized trial comparing ALPPS vs. PVL/PVE-TSH

## The LIGRO Trial Results

- **Resectability:** Higher in ALPPS (92% vs. 57%)
- **Safety:** Severe complications (43% vs 43%) and 90-day mortality (8.3% vs 6.1%) were statistically similar
- **Rescue:** ALPPS rescued 57% of failures in the TSH group
- **Survival:** Improved median survival for ALPPS (46 vs. 26 months)

## ALPPS for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)

- Challenging due to underlying cirrhosis and portal hypertension
- Initial registry data showed 31% 90-day mortality
- **Hong Kong University criteria** improved safety (6.5% mortality):
  - FLR < 30%, Child A, ICG R15 < 20%, Platelets > 100k
- Hypertrophy is somewhat less in cirrhotic livers, but complete transection yields faster hypertrophy than partial ALPPS
- **Anterior approach** with hanging maneuver is feasible and safe

## ALPPS for Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma (ICC)

- Early registry data showed high mortality (13-15%)
- Recent large single-center and multicenter studies show improved safety (7-8.3% mortality)
- 97% resectability rate, 85.3% R0 rate
- Better survival than chemotherapy for otherwise irresectable solitary ICC
- **Threshold:** FLR per body weight of 0.8% (or 40% TLV) recommended before Stage 2

## ALPPS for Perihilar Cholangiocarcinoma (PHC)

- Considered the **"Achilles' heel"** of ALPPS indications
- High risk due to devascularized parenchyma + infected bile/leaks
- 2017 case-matched analysis showed devastating 48% mortality vs 24% in PVE controls
- High mortality largely driven by the **initial learning curve** and use of Classic ALPPS
- **Mini ALPPS and Hybrid ALPPS** avoid hilar dissection in Stage 1 and show promise
- Widespread use outside expert high-volume centers is **not recommended**

## Summary: A Decade of ALPPS

- Over 10 years since the first procedure by Hans Jürgen Schlitt
- Early enthusiasm was hampered by high morbidity/mortality
- Continuous efforts improved:
  - Patient selection
  - Timing of Stage 2
  - Operative technique (minimizing Stage 1 trauma)
- ALPPS is now a **milestone in HPB surgery** for accelerating liver hypertrophy

## Summary: The Right Tool for the Right Patient

- ALPPS does **not** replace PVE or standard TSH
- It allows tumor resection in selected patients with no other surgical options
- **Benchmark cases** (younger age, high-volume center, CRLM) yield standard outcome measures
- Technical refinements may soon enable safer use in challenging entities like HCC and PHC
- ALPPS has earned its place in the armamentarium of experienced hepatobiliary surgeons
